Blumofe and Leiserson 1999, Theorem 1: any greedy P-processor schedule achieves T <= T1/P + T_inf, universally optimal to within a factor of 2, and gives linear speed-up when T1/T_inf = Omega(P); the model assumes zero cost to find and start a task and is loose by up to 2x.

Graham 1966 (Bell System Tech. J. 45(9)): an increase in the number of processing units can increase the total time needed to process a fixed set of tasks.

Graham 1966: four changes (the task list, task times, the partial order, the processor count) can each lengthen a list schedule, and 'easy counterexamples show' that shortening is not always the case.
Graham 1966: under those four changes the finishing time grows by at most a factor 1 + (n - 1)/n', the best possible bound; for n = n' and any list the factor is 2 - 1/n.
note: The OCR of this formula is garbled; the file reads it as 1 + (n - 1)/n'.

claim: Graham 1966: with no precedence constraints the list bound improves to 4/3 - 1/(3n), which the paper calls best possible.

Amdahl 1967: data-management housekeeping, about 40% of executed instructions in production runs, is sequential and would cap throughput at five to seven times the sequential processing rate.
Amdahl 1967 conclusion: effort on high parallel processing rates is wasted unless accompanied by sequential processing gains of very nearly the same magnitude.
Amdahl 1967 gives a probable region of 25% data-management overhead and 10% of the problem operations forced to be sequential.
Gunther arXiv 0808.1431 (eqs 2-3, a later formulation of Amdahl's law): S_p(alpha) = p / (1 + alpha (p - 1)), approaching 1/alpha as p grows.

claim: Gustafson 1988 (CACM 31(5)): scaled speed-up = s' + p' x N = N + (1 - N) x s', with s' and p' the serial and parallel times on the parallel system and N the processor count; the premise is that run time, not problem size, is constant.

Gustafson 1988 measured on a 1024-processor hypercube: speed-ups of 1021 (beam stress analysis), 1020 (baffled surface wave simulation) and 1016 (unstable fluid flow), for serial parts s = 0.4 to 0.8 percent.

Gunther arXiv 0808.1431 (Universal Scalability Law): C_p(alpha, beta) = p / (1 + alpha (p - 1) + beta p (p - 1)), with alpha the contention term and beta the coherency term; alpha and beta both zero is ideal linear scaling.
Gunther arXiv 0808.1431: the USL throughput has a maximum at p* = sqrt((1 - alpha)/beta), beyond which throughput becomes retrograde.

Jefferson 1985 (Time Warp): each process 'is constantly gambling' that no message arrives with an earlier virtual time, and pays a performance penalty by rolling back when the bet is lost.
Jefferson 1985 (Time Warp): the worst case of rollback is that all processes roll back to the same virtual time as the original one did; he denies a 'domino effect' beyond that bound.
note: Cascades within the bound exist; the file says unbounded ones do not.

claim: Jefferson 1985 conjectures that most programs obey a temporal locality principle, so most messages arrive in the virtual future and cause no rollback, and says this can only be verified empirically.
Jefferson 1985: the cost of virtual-time synchronisation is only the rollback and antimessage overhead, not the rolled-back computation, when compared with blocking.
note: The file adds that this comparison holds only if the processor would otherwise idle; that condition is the writer's remark at line 129, not Jefferson's.

claim: Jefferson 1985: saved state older than global virtual time (GVT) can be freed, and states and messages at or after GVT must be retained.
